statement: As described in a narrative review (Angarita et al., 2016; figures second-hand, no systematic search or appraisal), in people dependent on heroin or other opioids sleep is disturbed during regular use and in the weeks after stopping: in cited sleep-laboratory studies, the first week of abstinence from heroin brought shorter sleep, less deep (slow-wave) and REM sleep, longer time to fall asleep and more waking than in healthy sleepers, and over the first three weeks time to fall asleep was still long and sleep less efficient. In methadone maintenance more than three-quarters of people reported sleep complaints and about half used illicit drugs or medicines to help them sleep; long-term opioid use was linked with pauses in breathing during sleep (signs of central sleep apnoea in 30 to 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy), and buprenorphine treatment with sleep-disordered breathing in one study of 70 patients. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review of sleep research says that people coming off heroin sleep less and more lightly for weeks, and take longer to fall asleep. Many people on methadone also sleep badly, and long-term opioid use can cause pauses in breathing during sleep. The review did not check the studies' quality, so these are second-hand findings.
population: People with opioid use disorder (heroin; methadone or buprenorphine treatment; long-term opioid therapy), in studies cited by a narrative review
exposure: Regular opioid use and abstinence after it
comparator: Healthy sleepers or the same people at other times, as in the cited studies
outcome: Polysomnographic and self-reported sleep, sleep-disordered breathing
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized: early abstinence from heroin with reduced total, slow-wave and REM sleep and increased sleep latency and waking (Howe et al.); prolonged sleep latency and reduced efficiency over the first three weeks (Asaad et al.); sleep complaints in more than three-quarters of people in methadone maintenance, about half using drugs or medicines to sleep; central apnoea signs in 30 to 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy.

evidence.locator: Opioids › Objective measurements, 4th paragraph; Opioids › Subjective measurements, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: As summarized: at about the end of the first week of abstinence from heroin, total sleep time, slow-wave, REM and stage 2 sleep were reduced and sleep latency, wake after sleep onset and REM latency increased compared with healthy sleepers (Howe et al.); during the first three weeks of abstinence, prolonged sleep latency, reduced efficiency and total sleep, more arousals and less slow-wave sleep compared with healthy sleepers (Asaad et al.); after six weeks to six months of abstinence from methadone, slow-wave and REM sleep rebounded above baseline.

evidence.locator: Opioids › Opioids and sleep disordered breathing, 1st paragraph; Methadone, 1st paragraph; Buprenorphine, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: As summarized: more than three-quarters of people in methadone maintenance report sleep complaints and about 50% report using both illicit drugs and legal medications to help with sleep; between 30 and 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy show signs of central apnoea in a dose-dependent way; buprenorphine treatment in 70 patients with chronic opioid use was associated with mild to severe sleep-disordered breathing with a substantial rate of hypoxaemia.
The authors describe the paper as a narrative, non-systematic review of human clinical studies; no selection criteria, numbers or appraisal are given.

risk_of_bias.note: The cited studies are not appraisable through a narrative review.

indirectness.note: Second-hand figures from a narrative review.

grade.reasoning: Observational sleep studies start low; seen only through a narrative review, they are rated down for risk of bias and indirectness (METHODS 6.3), giving very low. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays draft and out of the at-a-glance box. Status replicated as described: at least two cited polysomnography studies (Howe et al.; Asaad et al.) point the same way; their independence could not be checked.
